sources: University of Arkansas Arthropod Museum, House centipede (Scutigera coleoptrata): jaws not powerful enough to break human skin easily; will sometimes bite in self-defense; not aggressive; severe swelling and pain can result, but in most cases the bite is no worse than the sting of a bee; captures prey by half pouncing and half lassoing; can capture several prey items at one time, feeding on one while holding the others; well-developed faceted eyes unlike most other centipedes; darts at high speed, stops suddenly and stays motionless, then races off; reached Pennsylvania 1849, New York 1885, Massachusetts about 1890, now westward to the Rocky Mountains and beyond; lab females laid an average of 63 eggs (max 151); indoors in bathrooms, moist closets, cellars, crawl spaces and piles of firewood; eats cockroach nymphs, flies, moths, bedbugs, crickets, silverfish, earwigs; https://arthropod.uark.edu/?p=27355

Connecticut Agricultural Experiment Station, House Centipede fact sheet (K. Dugas): forcipules (pincer-like modified legs) directly underneath the mouthparts give the venomous sting; can cause temporary localized pain; a sting to a human is very rare and the result of rough handling; reduce humidity by running fans or dehumidifiers; https://portal.ct.gov/-/media/caes/documents/publications/fact_sheets/entomology/house_centipede_scutigera.pdf

Washington State University PestSense, House centipede: runs very quickly holding its body up on its long legs; found in basements, bathrooms, closets or potted plants; use a vacuum to dispose of centipedes indoors; keep screens in good repair to reduce the insects it eats; https://pestsense.cahnrs.wsu.edu/fact-sheet/house-centipede/
Penn State Extension, House Centipedes (S. Jacobs): harmless; feeds on silverfish, firebrats, carpet beetle larvae, cockroaches, spiders; https://extension.psu.edu/house-centipedes

beats.say: It can bite you like a bee sting. And it lives in your bathroom.
It pounces, then lassoes bugs with its legs.
It can hold a few bugs at once, while it eats one.
Good news? Its jaws can barely break your skin.
